planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in late summer in a hot, sharply drained site; this diminutive relative of Sternbergia lutea wants a thorough summer baking to flower well and resents wet, heavy soils.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in late summer in lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil in full sun, ideally at the base of a south-facing wall or on a gravelly slope. This dwarf Sicilian and Balkan native produces small, glossy, star-shaped golden-yellow flowers close to the ground in early to mid fall, appearing just before or alongside the narrow grass-like leaves. It is smaller in every part than Sternbergia lutea, making it a choice subject for troughs, raised beds, and rock gardens where its diminutive scale can be appreciated up close. Leave clumps undisturbed for years, since the bulbs resent lifting and flower best when left to bake dry through summer dormancy.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in early fall in a sharply drained raised bed, trough, or bulb frame; this rare Turkish endemic flowers in late winter into spring and needs bone-dry summer dormancy rather than the baked-then-autumn-rain cycle of its yellow-flowered relatives.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in gritty, humus-poor, sharply drained soil in full sun, protecting the crown from prolonged winter wet with a raised bed, trough, or cold frame in climates with rainy winters. Unique among sternbergias for its sweetly scented, pure white, crocus-like flowers, this rare southwestern Turkish species blooms in late winter to early spring rather than autumn, following its strap-shaped leaves rather than preceding them. It is far less common in cultivation than the yellow-flowered species and considered vulnerable in the wild from over-collection, so bulbs should only be sourced from nursery propagation. Give it a hot, dry summer rest and minimal disturbance once established for the best chance of flowering.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall, or divide and move clumps 'in the green' just after flowering, into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich soil in dappled shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Found in 1993 and now a modern classic among galanthophiles, this pleated-leaf snowdrop cultivar is prized for its unusually heavy, quilted texture and squared-off, pear-shaped outer segments, giving each flower a distinctly sculptural look compared to ordinary snowdrops. Like other Galanthus plicatus selections, its wide, folded-back leaf margins distinguish it easily from Galanthus nivalis even before it flowers. Divide congested clumps in the green immediately after bloom and replant promptly, as the bulbs dislike prolonged drying out of the roots.

common_name: Flocon de Neige Snowdrop (French Double Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade; this late-flowering double selection increases slowly, so start with nursery-propagated stock rather than dividing right away.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Selected in Buckinghamshire in the mid-1980s and named for its resemblance to a six-pointed snowflake when viewed from above, this double form of the common snowdrop carries six neat, uniform outer segments surrounding a tidy inner rosette of extra petal-like segments. It flowers later than most single snowdrops, typically in late February and March, extending the snowdrop season into early spring. Growth is steady but unhurried, so leave clumps undisturbed for several years to bulk up before dividing in the green after flowering.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this Award of Garden Merit selection from the Greek mountains naturalizes readily in lawns, gravel gardens, and rock gardens.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade. One of the earliest crocus to bloom, this named selection of Crocus sieberi subsp. sublimis from the Greek mountains opens goblet-shaped flowers banded in three distinct colors: a bright golden-yellow throat, a crisp white ring, and lilac-purple petal tips. Like other Crocus sieberi forms, the flowers close on dull days and open fully only in direct sun, and the grass-like foliage should be allowed to yellow naturally after bloom before any tidying. It multiplies steadily by offsets and self-sows lightly, making broadening drifts in rock gardens, troughs, and lawns over time.

common_name: Ladykiller Crocus (Purple and White Snow Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; this heirloom snow crocus is among the earliest to bloom, often flowering ahead of the large Dutch crocus.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained soil in full sun. This Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit heirloom carries a bold bicolor contrast unusual among snow crocus, with deep purple-violet outer petals sharply edged in white enclosing a pure white interior and vivid orange stamens. It is one of the earliest crocus to flower, often opening in late winter well before the large-flowered Dutch types, and naturalizes readily into expanding clumps in rock gardens, lawns, and border edges. Leave the grass-like foliage to die back naturally after bloom to recharge the corms for the following season.
